content.p: On the night of 27 February 1947, a confrontation over illegal cigarettes on a Taipei street ended with a bystander shot dead by a government agent. The next morning, crowds marched on government offices. Within days the protests had spread across the island, and the Nationalist government of the Republic of China answered with troops brought in from the mainland. The episode came to be known as the 228 Incident, after its date. Taiwan's government later apologised for it, but the number of people who died remains disputed.

Japan had ruled Taiwan from 1895 until its surrender in 1945. Under Japanese rule the island's infrastructure and economy had been developed, and many Taiwanese had a comparatively favourable view of that period. After the war the island was handed to the Nationalist government under General Chiang Kai-shek, and Chen Yi became its governor-general.

OFTaiwan's history of the incident says Chen took control of the state monopolies Japan had run over crops and goods. He used that power to buy goods cheaply and ship them to mainland China, where shortages during the civil war sold at high prices. Officials from the mainland filled many government posts, and undisciplined Nationalist troops looted and damaged infrastructure the Japanese had built. Unemployment, inflation and corruption fed a growing anger.

The 228 Incident Memorial Foundation, which the government later created to handle compensation, describes the same period in similar terms. It says Chen brought "rule by man" and discrimination against local people to the island, and that poor conduct by his officials and a worsening economy stoked public discontent.

OFTaiwan gives the most detailed account of the first incident. On the night of 27 February, agents from the Tobacco Monopoly Bureau tried to seize contraband cigarettes from a woman in her forties who sold them outside a tea house in Taipei. When she asked for her money and her cigarettes back, one agent beat her on the head with his pistol. A crowd gathered to confront the agents over the force they had used. As the agents withdrew, one of them fired into the crowd and killed a bystander.

The New York Times, reporting on a museum guide's account of the events in 2015, gives the same sequence: an official struck the woman on the head with the butt of a pistol, and that set off the anger of the Taiwanese people. The Foundation describes the death differently. It says the agents "accidentally" shot and killed an innocent passerby while beating the female vendor. OFTaiwan and the Foundation agree that a bystander died, but they differ on whether the shot was deliberate and on the sequence of events. Neither account resolves the question.

On 28 February, crowds marched on the Tobacco Monopoly Bureau to demand that the government hand over the agents involved. When protesters gathered at the governor-general's office, its guards opened fire, according to OFTaiwan. The Foundation says the protesters were shot by law enforcement officers and that casualties were reported. The violence turned into an open revolt that lasted several weeks.

Local leaders then formed a settlement committee. Its list of demands, which OFTaiwan calls the "32 Demands", asked for greater autonomy for the province, free elections and an end to official corruption. The Foundation says the committee called for reform, and that the government's response was to call in troops. The New York Times's 2015 account says that within days Taiwanese had taken over much of the island's administration.

OFTaiwan dates the arrival of reinforcements from the Nationalist army to 8 March 1947. The Foundation describes Chen as regarding the local leaders as "a bunch of bandits and mobsters", and says that he called in troops from mainland China to put the revolt down. The Foundation says that calling in the troops took a heavy toll on people's lives and property in the months afterwards, and that a "white terror" purge in rural areas followed.

OFTaiwan says that by the end of March Chen had ordered the imprisonment or execution of every Taiwanese organiser he could identify, and that this killed between 3,000 and 4,000 people across the island. The New York Times wrote that the troops killed thousands in a spree that began four decades of white terror, a campaign against Nationalist opponents, principally Communists, that lasted until martial law was lifted in 1987. The Taipei Times puts the declaration of martial law on 4 March, which is before the troops' main crackdown.

The Taipei Times's 2016 series on the newspaper purge after the incident shows how the official line hardened. The government-owned Taiwan Shin Sheng Daily News first criticised the Tobacco Monopoly Bureau for going after illegal vendors instead of smugglers, and said that the agents had no need to carry guns. Its editorial of 28 March 1947, headed "228 Was Not a Civil Uprising", described the uprising as the work of "scheming traitors with political ambition along with lackeys of the former Japanese government", with followers who were "local hoodlums, gangsters and students".

By then the paper had new management: a major-general with the Taiwan Garrison Command as general manager, and an adviser from the provincial administration as editor-in-chief. The Taipei Times reports that the former manager, Juan Chao-jih, and the former deputy editor-in-chief, Wu Chin-lien, along with several other staff members, had been missing for nearly two weeks by 25 March.

The New York Times described one individual case in 1992. Lin Mao-sheng, who was a dean at National Taiwan University and held an American doctorate, the first of its kind earned by a Taiwanese, was summoned one March day by two plainclothes officers, who summoned him to a meeting with the provincial governor. His family never saw him again. The newspaper described him as one of thousands killed in the massacre, and the article does not say who gave the orders for his detention.

For decades the subject was almost impossible to raise. OFTaiwan says the government kept its records on the incident classified as "top secret" even after martial law ended in 1987, and that speaking about the event was considered taboo. It also says the massacre went unacknowledged for 48 years, until President Lee Teng-hui apologised on the government's behalf in 1995. The New York Times said in 1992 that almost no one dared mention the massacre in public until a few years earlier.

Taiwan's government did act. In 1990 it formed a commission of Taiwanese and foreign specialists to examine the events and gather the relevant files. The panel reported in 1992. According to the Taipei Times in 2007, the report concluded that Chiang Kai-shek should take responsibility for the incident. The New York Times reported that the report's drafter, Lai Tse-han, found no hard evidence that either Chiang directly planned the massacre. The Foundation was created in October 1995 to examine victims' claims, pay compensation, restore victims' reputations and investigate what happened. A monument was put up in the 228 Memorial Park in Taipei the same year. OFTaiwan adds that President Tsai Ing-wen later declassified documents on the incident and promised further government investigation.

The figures differ by source, and each one comes from a different place. OFTaiwan's introduction describes the revolt as having resulted in "tens of thousands of deaths", while its account of the crackdown under Chen gives 3,000 to 4,000 killed. The 1992 report, which the New York Times described as officially backed, suggested that 18,000 to 28,000 people may have died; Marvin C. H. Ho, a commission member, told the New York Times that he and most members did not subscribe to so high a range. A museum volunteer quoted by the New York Times in 2015 spoke of "as many as 28,000" killed in 1947. Ho also said that the government had not interfered with the work, which he described as unusual in the writing of Chinese history.

In 2007 Premier Su Tseng-chang announced that the Foundation's report would be treated as an official document, and that the Foundation would become a permanent government body. The Taipei Times reported that the cabinet also agreed that the national flag would fly at half-mast on 28 February every year. The Taipei Times also reported that under the original regulations the Foundation was due to be disbanded in June 2010.

The Taipei 228 Memorial Museum opened in 1997 in a building that had housed the government's radio broadcasting bureau during the Japanese period. Its park stands near the centre of the capital and lies within walking distance of the Presidential Palace. The Uni Jena summary of the anniversary describes 28 February as a national day of remembrance and says that the reappraisal of the events reflects a new view of Taiwan's own history, which began with a presidential decree in 1995.

President Lai Ching-te attended the main memorial ceremony for the 78th anniversary, and apologised again on behalf of the nation. His office's account of the speech says he promised to make political archives available to the public, to clarify the facts of history and to pursue transitional justice. He also paid tribute to Lin Tsai-shou, the founding chairman of the Changhua County 228 Incident Care Association, who had recently died.

The date has a second, separate tragedy. The University of Jena notes that on 28 February 1980 the mother and siblings of the human rights lawyer Lin I-hsiung were killed at their home. Lin was in prison at the time, and the house was under strict surveillance, yet an intruder got in. The Jena account does not say who was responsible.
